title: continuous-batching-scheduler-tuning-experiments-3
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a round of continuous-batching scheduler tuning experiments focused on: max batch size, max wait (timeout), scheduling fairness across model families, and 99th/99.9th tail latency behavior. Goal is to find knob settings that reduce p99 tail while keeping throughput high and cost per token reasonable for typical Redwood-hosted API workloads.

Background / context (notes to self):
- Prior baseline (see experiments-1/2) used max_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=50, fairness=round_robin across model variants. Observed good average latency but p99 spikes under bursty traffic (short sequences + many concurrent users).
- Workloads representative of production: fed with 3 workload mixes:
  * QA short (avg tokens per request ~ 60, high rps)
  * Chat medium (avg tokens ~ 200, moderate rps)
  * Long generation (avg tokens ~ 1200, low rps)
- Testbed: 4x A100 instance pool, runtime commit: serving-runtime@2024-10-31 (baseline), OS/container stable. KV cache enabled for prefix reuse when applicable.

Methodology / test harness:
- Used the synthetic traffic generator (tools/loadgen) seeded with traces from production (sanitized), replayed at 1x, 2x, 5x baseline load. Each run lasted 30 minutes with 10 minute warmup.
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 latency (server side, end-to-end), throughput (tokens/sec), batching efficiency (avg batch size, batch wait distribution), GPU utilization, and fairness metrics (per-tenant latency variance).
- For each parameter set we repeated runs 3x and report median of medians.

Scheduler knobs explored:
- max_batch_size: [8, 16, 32, 64]
- max_wait_ms: [10, 25, 50, 100] (timeout for flushing a partially filled batch)
- fairness: [round_robin, weighted_priority, latency_based]
- tail_smoothing: [on/off] (experimental smoothing to avoid huge batches causing long queuing times for subsequent small requests)

Key experimental runs (high level):
1) Baseline: mb=32, wait=50, fairness=round_robin, tail_smoothing=off
2) Small-batches: mb=16, wait=25, fairness=round_robin
3) Aggressive batching: mb=64, wait=100, fairness=weighted_priority
4) Low-latency mode: mb=8, wait=10, fairness=latency_based, tail_smoothing=on
5) Hybrid: mb=32, wait=25, fairness=weighted_priority, tail_smoothing=on

Representative results (aggregated):
- Baseline (32/50/rr): throughput=120k tokens/sec, p99=420ms, p99.9=980ms, avg_batch_size=27
- Small-batches (16/25/rr): throughput=107k tokens/sec (-11%), p99=260ms (-38%), p99.9=650ms (-34%), avg_batch_size=13
- Aggressive (64/100/wp): throughput=135k tokens/sec (+12%), p99=540ms (+29%), p99.9=1550ms (+58%), avg_batch_size=50
- Low-latency (8/10/lat): throughput=92k tokens/sec (-23%), p99=190ms (-55%), p99.9=480ms (-51%), avg_batch_size=6
- Hybrid (32/25/wp/on): throughput=122k tokens/sec (+2%), p99=300ms (-29%), p99.9=720ms (-26%), avg_batch_size=22

Observations / interpretation:
- There is a clear tradeoff between throughput and tail latency. Larger max_batch_size + longer wait increases throughput but amplifies p99/p99.9 dramatically due to head-of-line blocking when a large long-running request joins a batch.
- Small-batches & low-latency configurations reduce tail significantly but at material throughput cost and higher per-token CPU/GPU utilization (less batching efficiency). For latency-sensitive endpoints (chat front-end) this is acceptable.
- Hybrid (same max_batch_size but slightly lower wait and weighted priority) gives a good middle ground: small reduction in throughput but substantial tail improvements. Weighted priority which biases shorter sequences to flush earlier reduces head-of-line blocking.
- tail_smoothing=on reduced p99.9 for mixed workloads by ~10-15% in most runs; the heuristic (limit single-request contribution to batch max wait when expected sequence length > threshold) prevented very large batches from indefinitely delaying short sequences. More tuning needed.
- Fairness: round_robin caused per-tenant variance under bursty traffic. weighted_priority reduced variance but requires accurate per-request cost estimation (tokens/expected runtime). latency_based scheduling improved p95 but sometimes starved heavy long-running requests if not throttled.

Quick notes on KV-cache interaction:
- When KV cache hits are frequent (chat with repeated prefixes), batching benefits are amplified because effective per-request compute drops and more requests can aggregate. But tail spikes still occur when a cache-miss long generation is co-batched.
- Consider tagging requests with cache-hit hint so scheduler can avoid co-batching cold requests with hot ones.

Cost/throughput economics (rough):
- Aggressive batching reduces GPU-seconds per token by ~8-12% vs baseline, but increases SLA risk (higher p99 penalties).
- Low-latency mode increases GPU-seconds per token ~18-25%, better for premium tiers where latency SLOs are required.

Recommendations (short-term):
1) Introduce a "latency-sensitive" route config (per-API route) that switches to lower max_batch_size (8-16) and lower max_wait (10-25ms). Make default for chat endpoints.
2) Default scheduler: Hybrid preset (mb=32, wait=25, fairness=weighted_priority, tail_smoothing=on). Gives balanced throughput and tail.
3) Implement request tagging for KV-cache hints so scheduler can avoid co-batching cold long-run requests with hot short-run ones.
4) Improve cost model: runtime should estimate expected token cost at enqueue time (cheap heuristic: avg_tokens_from_prompt or model-provided estimate) and use it in weighted_priority.
5) Add p99.9 shadowing for any aggressive-batching change in prod for 2 weeks before rollouts - will detect rare extreme tails.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How sensitive are results to sequence length mix drift? Need longer-run tests with diurnal patterns and correlated bursts (user think-time patterns).
- Weighted_priority depends on good cost estimates; what is acceptable error tolerance? We should run ablation with noisy estimates (+/- 50%).
- Explore dynamic wait: instead of fixed max_wait_ms, use adaptive wait based on recent queue latency distribution. Prototype idea started in github PR linked above.
- Need SRE input on p99.9 alerting thresholds and rollback policies for new scheduler presets.
